claims.sentence: CT measures attenuation directly, and so can replace the radionuclide transmission scan that earlier PET systems required \cite{Kinahan1998}\claim*{Kinahan1998/a74191}.

A piecewise-linear rescaling of Hounsfield units is consequently applied, interpolating between air and water below the breakpoint and between water and cortical bone above it, to convert the CT image into a \keV{511} attenuation map \cite{Burger2002,Carney2006}\claim*{Burger2002/0f14c7,Carney2006/ce68d7,Carney2006/85b1a2}.

Of the two dominant losses, solid angle and attenuation in the patient, only solid angle is a design choice rather than a fixed cost of imaging a human, coverage ranging from the order of \qty{20}{\percent} in a conventional ring to as much as \qty{80}{\percent} in long axial field-of-view scanners \cite{Vandenberghe2020}\claim*{Vandenberghe2020/8338ba,Vandenberghe2020/7f38d9}.

\paragraph{Origins} Positrons were discovered in 1932 by Carl Anderson, who observed the tracks of seemingly positively-charged electrons in a cloud chamber and interpreted them as the electron's antimatter counterpart \cite{Anderson1933}\claim*{Anderson1933/9b56e8}.

Wrenn and colleagues proposed using the back-to-back annihilation photons for coincidence localisation in 1951 \cite{Wrenn1951}\claim*{Wrenn1951/18681d}, and Brownell and Sweet built one of the first clinical positron scanners in 1953, comprised of a pair of sodium iodide detectors stepped mechanically across the head on a rectilinear gantry \cite{Sweet1953}.

Anger's scintillation camera of 1958 replaced mechanical scanning with a single large NaI(Tl) crystal viewed by an array of photomultiplier tubes, positioning each event from the centroid of the light distribution \cite{Anger1958}\claim*{Anger1958/dd2514,Anger1958/c7bb16}, a stationary-detector, position-decoding architecture that PET block detectors would later inherit.

Kuhl and Edwards then demonstrated emission tomography itself in 1963, rotating a scanner about the patient and reconstructing transverse sections from the resulting projections \cite{Kuhl1963}, several years before the equivalent was achieved with transmission X-rays \cite{Hounsfield1973}\claim*{Hounsfield1973/fc8eab}.

\paragraph{The Move to Tomographic Rings} In 1961, a group at Brookhaven National Laboratory developed a ring of 32 sodium iodide-based coincidence detectors surrounding the head \cite{Rankowitz1961}\claim*{Rankowitz1961/e416c7}.

By the late 1960s Brownell and the group at Massachusetts General Hospital had developed a so-called ``hybrid scanner'' comprised of two stationary planar 2D arrays of detectors, and by the early 1970s the group had developed a device of similar architecture known as the ``multi-crystal positron camera'', which had a field of view of $\cm{27}\times\cm{30}$ \cite{Burnham1972}\claim*{Burnham1972/026348,Burnham1972/5b5093}.

The projections this produced were of exactly the form that filtered backprojection had been developed to invert, and the reconstruction was imported essentially intact from the single-photon and X-ray tomography described above \cite{Phelps1975}\claim*{Phelps1975/514189,Phelps1975/158f7c}.
The synthesis of \textsuperscript{18}F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) in 1976 removed that constraint \cite{Ido1978}\claim*{Ido1978/dbe5a1}.

\paragraph{The Block Detector} The block detector, introduced by Casey and Nutt in 1986 \cite{Casey1986}\claim*{Casey1986/9a954e}, in response to increasing demand, shifted focus towards cost-effective detector architectures to maximise the clinical utility of PET.

\paragraph{Scintillators, Timing and Scale} In the 1980s, available fast-response scintillators such as BaF\textsubscript{2} and CsF successfully demonstrated the advantages of time-of-flight (TOF) PET, but they had drawbacks, notably low density and low photofraction, which compromised performance enough for BGO to continue as the dominant PET scintillator \cite{Moses2007}\claim*{Moses2007/37c442,Moses2007/97543d}.

Lutetium oxyorthosilicate (LSO) in the late 1980s, and lutetium--yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) by the early 2000s, delivered the faster decay times that TOF-PET demanded without the density and photofraction drawbacks of predecessor scintillators, effectively reviving the technique and gaining popularity over BGO in spite of their slightly higher price \cite{Moses2007}\claim*{Moses2007/a66733,Moses2007/42cbcd}.

Most recently, long axial field-of-view systems such as the uEXPLORER and the Biograph Quadra have raised sensitivity by an order of magnitude by extending the axial length of the scanner to cover the whole body \cite{Vandenberghe2020, SLHD2021}\claim*{Vandenberghe2020/1641db,SLHD2021/44acb4}.

The pair is not quite at rest, however, and its residual momentum spreads the opening angle about \degs{180} with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of roughly \degs{0.5} \cite{Colombino1965}\claim*{Colombino1965/44f285}.

\paragraph{Annihilation and Coincidence Detection} Over time, the radionuclide decays, emitting positrons, which travel a short distance known as the positron range before annihilating with an electron and producing two approximately collinear \keV{511} annihilation photons, a small fraction of which escape the subject's body without scattering and are detected by the PET scanner.

The positron range depends on the emitter, from sub-millimetre for fluorine-18 to several millimetres for higher-energy emitters such as rubidium-82, and the residual momentum of the electron--positron pair at annihilation spreads the opening angle about \degs{180} with a full width at half maximum of roughly \degs{0.5} \needcite{positron range by emitter and the acollinearity FWHM}.
However, it does so at the effective energy of the polychromatic X-ray beam ($\sim$\keV{70} at a tube voltage of 120\,kV \needcite{effective CT beam energy at 120 kVp}) rather than at \keV{511}.

The attenuation coefficients at the two energies are not related by a single scale factor, since the photoelectric contribution is non-negligible in higher-Z materials such as bone and iodinated contrast agents, and scales steeply with atomic number, whereas at \keV{511} it is negligible and attenuation is governed almost entirely by electron density.
Two materials sharing a value in Hounsfield units (HU), the CT measure of radiodensity, may therefore differ in their attenuation at \keV{511}.

Tomography thus reached PET second-hand, since the ring scanners of the 1970s combined coincidence detection, already established, with reconstruction mathematics developed for single-photon and X-ray imaging.
The \mins{110} half-life of \textsuperscript{18}F is long enough to permit production at a cyclotron some distance from the scanner.

In the decades that followed, removing the septa between axially stacked detector rings and acquiring in fully-3D raised sensitivity several-fold at the cost of a much larger scattered fraction, and increasingly necessitated corrective algorithms to resolve it.

Silicon photomultipliers, developed over the late 1990s and 2000s, had by the early 2010s matured enough to warrant their adoption over traditional photomultiplier tubes, improving timing, compactness, and permitting operation inside a magnetic field.

That annihilation converts the rest mass of the particle and anti-particle into two high-energy photons, each of \keV{511} in accordance with the energy--mass equivalence defined by $E=mc^2$.

Projected onto a detector ring of diameter $D$, this acollinearity contributes a positional blur that grows linearly with the diameter, approximately $0.0022D$ FWHM \needcite{the 0.0022D acollinearity blur}, so it is a modest penalty in preclinical systems but a leading resolution term in large-bore clinical scanners.
Earlier BGO-based scanners, with substantially poorer intrinsic timing, required windows of 10--12\,ns \needcite{coincidence windows of BGO-based scanners}.

\subsection{Radionuclides and Radiotracers} \label{sec:radiotracers} \topics{brief, for context only: cyclotron isotopes (\textsuperscript{18}F, \textsuperscript{11}C) and generator isotopes (\textsuperscript{68}Ga, \textsuperscript{82}Rb) and the half-life logistics that tie a scanner to its tracer supply; FDG as the workhorse and the targeted tracers (PSMA, amyloid and tau) that are widening demand; the one cost point that matters here: tracer supply is a cost lever independent of the scanner, so scanner cost is the lever this thesis pulls.}

Resolution limits: positron range; $\sim$0.25\textdegree{} acollinearity and its ring-diameter dependence; detector pitch; the resolution budget in quadrature; why sub-mm whole-body PET is physics-limited.

Photon interactions: Beer--Lambert $I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}$, the basis of attenuation correction and the Siddon path integrals (\S\ref{sec:system-matrix}); photoelectric absorption and its steep effective-$Z$ dependence, the crux of plastic versus inorganic (\S\ref{sec:organic}); Compton scatter, $E' = E/[1 + (E/m_ec^2)(1-\cos\theta)]$ and the Klein--Nishina cross-section as working tools for the multi-vertex/Compton-camera direction; Compton dominance at \keV{511} and its implications for detector thickness, inter-crystal scatter and sensitivity.}

\subsection{Scintillation Mechanisms and Figures of Merit} \label{sec:scintillation-mechanisms} \topics{three distinct mechanisms: inorganic scintillation via band structure and activator dopants, organic via molecular $\pi$-electron singlets, noble-element excimers as the third -- why the families behave so differently at \keV{511}.

Within the inorganics the luminescence transition predicts timing: self-activated (BGO, PWO, CdWO\textsubscript{4}), 5d$\rightarrow$4f (Ce\textsuperscript{3+}, Pr\textsuperscript{3+}), s\textsuperscript{2}-ion (Tl\textsuperscript{+}, Eu\textsuperscript{2+}), core--valence (BaF\textsubscript{2}); only 5d$\rightarrow$4f is dipole-allowed and fast, which explains the decay-time ordering better than any bulk property.

Then the figures of merit -- light yield, decay and rise time, density and effective Z, emission matching, energy resolution with non-proportionality as its dominant limit (why SrI\textsubscript{2}:Eu beats NaI(Tl) at comparable yield), afterglow, hygroscopicity, machinability -- and which actually matter for a cost-driven design.

In every scintillator the \keV{511} photon makes no light itself but, by photoelectric absorption or Compton scatter, liberates one energetic electron, and the light, its yield and its timing are the material's response to that electron.

These carriers then migrate, some binding into excitons and some lost to trapping or non-radiative quenching, until they are captured at luminescence centres (typically an activator dopant, Ce\textsuperscript{3+} in LSO and LYSO or Tl\textsuperscript{+} in NaI), where they recombine radiatively and emit many lower-energy optical photons (visible or near-visible light).

The number of electron--hole pairs created by a deposit of energy $E$ scales as $E/(\xi E_\mathrm{g})$, where $E_\mathrm{g}$ is the band gap of the host and $\xi \approx 2$--$3$ is the factor by which the average energy cost of one thermalised pair exceeds that gap, the excess being lost to the phonons emitted during thermalisation.

The intrinsic alternatives are a self-trapped exciton, where the pair distorts the lattice around itself and that relaxation takes energy out before emission (undoped CsI, the slow component of BaF\textsubscript{2}); a self-activated host, where a constituent ion of the lattice acts as its own centre with a large Stokes shift (Bi\textsuperscript{3+} in BGO, the tungstate group in PWO and CdWO\textsubscript{4}); core--valence luminescence, where a valence electron fills a core hole and the photon carries the core--valence spacing, smaller than the gap in the few crystals that show it, with no thermalised carriers involved at all (the sub-nanosecond fast component of BaF\textsubscript{2}, CsF); and, in direct-gap semiconductors and perovskites, a free or confined exciton, whose emission sits only just below the gap, so that self-absorption is a real limit and these are used thin or as nanocrystals.

By mechanism, then, the inorganic family takes in the halides (NaI:Tl, CsI:Tl, LaBr\textsubscript{3}:Ce, CeBr\textsubscript{3}, SrI\textsubscript{2}:Eu, BaF\textsubscript{2}), the oxides and garnets, among them BGO, LSO, LYSO and gadolinium aluminium gallium garnet (GAGG), whether grown as crystals or sintered as transparent ceramics, Ce-doped glasses, and the semiconductor and perovskite scintillators, the hybrid organic--inorganic perovskites included, since their light comes from the inorganic lead-halide framework and not from the organic cation.

The scintillating species is an aromatic hydrocarbon whose delocalised $\pi$-electron system supports a ladder of singlet ($S_0$, $S_1$, $S_2$, \dots) and triplet ($T_1$, \dots) states, each subdivided into vibrational sublevels.

The same fast electron, liberated by the \keV{511} photon as before, excites $\pi$ electrons into the upper singlets, which relax non-radiatively to $S_1$ by internal conversion within picoseconds; the $S_1 \rightarrow S_0$ transition then fluoresces in \qtyrange{1}{3}{\nano\second}.

Because fluorescence terminates on vibrationally excited sublevels of $S_0$, the emitted photon is lower in energy than the $S_0 \rightarrow S_1$ absorption and the material is transparent to its own light, the same requirement as before, here met by a vibrational offset where the inorganic uses an activator level inside the gap.

Intersystem crossing diverts some excitations to $T_1$, from which direct radiative decay (phosphorescence) is spin-forbidden, slow and dim, and what returns that energy as light is the bimolecular annihilation of two $T_1$ excitations, $T_1 + T_1 \rightarrow S_1 + S_0$, which regenerates $S_1$ so that the ordinary $S_1 \rightarrow S_0$ fluorescence occurs hundreds of nanoseconds late.
The triplet detour is the second route to the same $S_1 \rightarrow S_0$ emission.

Phosphorescence direct from $T_1$ is spin-forbidden and contributes little light, while annihilation of two triplets refills $S_1$ and the ordinary fluorescence then comes late, which is what pulse-shape discrimination reads.

As in any scintillator the \keV{511} photon itself makes no light but liberates one fast electron, which spends its energy along a track of a few millimetres ionising atoms (Xe $\rightarrow$ Xe\textsuperscript{+} + e\textsuperscript{$-$}, at about \qty{15.6}{\electronvolt} a pair) and exciting others (Xe $\rightarrow$ Xe\textsuperscript{*}).
An isolated excited atom would emit at \qty{147}{\nano\metre}, a resonance line that every neighbouring atom reabsorbs, so that light would never leave the liquid.

Instead, Xe\textsuperscript{*}, unlike a ground-state atom, binds a neighbour within picoseconds into the excimer Xe\textsubscript{2}\textsuperscript{*} (Ar\textsubscript{2}\textsuperscript{*} in argon), a two-atom molecule that exists only while it is excited, and the ions reach the same state by a longer route, Xe\textsuperscript{+} capturing first a neighbour and then an electron.
The excimer emits a vacuum-ultraviolet photon, at \qty{178}{\nano\metre} in xenon and \qty{128}{\nano\metre} in argon, and lands on a ground state that is unbound, so the pair falls apart.
With no ground-state dimer left to absorb at that wavelength, and the photon well below the \qty{147}{\nano\metre} atomic resonance in energy, the liquid is transparent to its own light.

As in the organic case the excimer has a singlet and a triplet state, and the two give a prompt and a slow component, a few nanoseconds against roughly \qty{27}{\nano\second} in xenon and against microseconds in argon, the ratio again depending on ionisation density.\needcite{Aprile and Doke 2010 review for excimer timing, yields and the recombination component}

The light yield is high, comparable to NaI(Tl) in liquid xenon, and liquid xenon's density and atomic number ($\qty{2.95}{\gram\per\centi\metre\cubed}$, $Z=54$) make it a respectable absorber at \keV{511}, so the mechanism is not dismissed on physics.
An excited atom, made directly or by recombination, binds a neighbour into the excimer Xe$_2^*$, which sits in a bound well.

\subsection{Inorganic Crystals and Ceramics} \label{sec:inorganic} \topics{property table across NaI(Tl), BGO, LSO:Ce, LYSO:Ce, GSO, BaF\textsubscript{2}, LaBr\textsubscript{3}.

Practical liabilities that disqualify materials the table flatters: \textsuperscript{176}Lu/\textsuperscript{138}La intrinsic radioactivity, hygroscopicity, thermal quenching (a cooling requirement, so a system cost), radiation damage, fragility.
The BGO renaissance for non-TOF high-sensitivity systems; Cherenkov and cross-luminescence (BaF\textsubscript{2}) as the materials-side response to the \ps{10} challenge.}

\subsection{Organic Scintillators: Plastics and Liquids} \label{sec:organic} \topics{why the molecular mechanism is fast but low-yield; the low effective-Z problem: photofraction collapses at \keV{511}, so interactions are overwhelmingly Compton; J-PET's response (Compton kinematics, axial plastic strips); manufacturability as the headline advantage -- no growth, no dicing, castable, cost per volume orders below LYSO; consequences for energy resolution and scatter rejection; the honest verdict on whether the cost win survives the sensitivity loss; a closing line on nanoparticle-loaded composites and metascintillators as the attempted middle ground (inorganic effective Z, organic manufacturability), still a promise rather than a result.}
A polyvinyltoluene-based plastic yields around \num{10000} photons per \unit{\mega\electronvolt} against roughly \num{38000} for NaI(Tl), and the deficit has several independent causes.

Ionisation quenching removes more: where the local energy-loss rate is high, excited molecules are quenched by damaged neighbours before they can fluoresce, an effect described empirically by Birks' law, \begin{equation} \frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{\eta \, \mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}x}{1 + k_\mathrm{B} \, \mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}x}, \label{eq:birks} \end{equation} in which $L$ is the emitted light, $\eta$ the scintillation efficiency in the unquenched limit, and $k_\mathrm{B} \approx \qty{0.1}{\milli\metre\per\mega\electronvolt}$ in plastic sets the energy-loss rate above which the response ceases to be proportional.
Cherenkov: prompt, hence the \ps{10} interest, but tens of photons and a directional cone (cross-reference \S\ref{sec:inorganic}).
Direct conversion (CdZnTe, TlBr): excellent energy resolution and intrinsic 3D positioning, against poor timing, charge trapping, and prohibitive cost at whole-body scale.

unclaimed.sentence: Wrenn and colleagues proposed using the back-to-back annihilation photons for coincidence localisation in 1951 \cite{Wrenn1951}\claim*{Wrenn1951/18681d}, and Brownell and Sweet built one of the first clinical positron scanners in 1953, comprised of a pair of sodium iodide detectors stepped mechanically across the head on a rectilinear gantry \cite{Sweet1953}.

Kuhl and Edwards then demonstrated emission tomography itself in 1963, rotating a scanner about the patient and reconstructing transverse sections from the resulting projections \cite{Kuhl1963}, several years before the equivalent was achieved with transmission X-rays \cite{Hounsfield1973}\claim*{Hounsfield1973/fc8eab}.

In the mid-1970s, Ter-Pogossian, Phelps and Hoffman built the positron emission transaxial tomograph (PETT) series, rings of scintillation detectors where every crystal was in coincidence with those opposite it, so that a single acquisition sampled the object along lines of response at many angles at once \cite{Ter-Pogossian1975}.
